title: Chicago
full_review:
Scaling the heights of razzle-dazzle theatricality is the movie musical "Chicago" (Miramax), starring a threesome not previously known for singing and dancing talents.

Catherine Zeta-Jones as vaudeville star Velma Kelly is terrific. She outshines the musical's lead star, Renee Zellweger. And, well, the less said about Richard Gere's singing and dancing the better. Nonetheless, this zesty adaptation of Bob Fosse's Broadway show is a spirited, toe-tapping melange of familiar show tunes and voluptuous visuals.

Theater purists, especially those who have been to the 1975 production and/or the successful 1997 revival of "Chicago," may find fault with the screen version. Choppy editing lends the impression that the film is fast-paced, but such quick cuts can undermine the musical's fluidity. And one may have preferred to get the whole picture of a dance number rather than crosscuts to close-ups of feet, hands and the performers' facial expressions. One hit song from the show, "Class," is dropped while another is added. All that said, the movie is a rousing crowd-pleaser that boldly jumps from stage to screen and doesn't look back.

It's set in Prohibition-era Chicago, where, early on, Velma takes center stage alone for a number usually performed with her singing sibling. Watching her enviously from the audience is chorus girl Roxie Hart (Zellweger). Suddenly, the cops burst in and arrest Velma, who's just rubbed out both her traitorous sister and her cheating husband.

Soon after Velma lands in the pokey she's followed by sweet-faced Roxie, who's knocked off her lying lover after he promised to further her career, then laughed in her face. Roxie's chump of a husband (John C. Reilly) was ready to take the fall for Roxie but the cops tricked her into admitting the dirty deed.

Enter money-lusting lawyer Billy Flynn (Gere), who's representing Velma, and now takes on Roxie, fabricating a poor, convent-bred-girl-fallen-low fiction about Roxie to win her notoriety and public sympathy before the trial. And Roxie's happy to use murder as the means to win fame; the musical numbers in the movie often spring from Roxie's imagining herself at the center of the spotlight.

Though Roxie and Velma spurn each other in jail out of jealousy, the public's short attention span for scandal requires them to team up to keep the spotlight.

Fosse's Broadway musical was originally based on Maurine Dallas Watkins' 1926 dramatic play, but director Rob Marshall's energetic adaptation brings out the black comedy elements of the piece. The movie takes on a naughty tone with Velma and Roxie seen as anti-heroines and everyone winking at the rampant corruption in a city where murder is regarded as entertainment.

Queen Latifah is introduced in a dynamite production number as the opportunistic but sympathetic prison matron who shows a deft hand for comedy as well.

Zellweger is game to sing and dance, but her puffy face atop a very skinny body appear at odds, especially when seen alongside robust-looking Zeta-Jones. Yet in her fantasy sequences Zellweger is photographed so glamorously with the platinum hairdo and ruby red lips that she looks like the "preincarnation" of Marilyn Monroe. Where she excels is in conveying her character's surface innocence, which hides her cold and calculating ambition.

Movie musicals being few and far between these days, "Chicago," with its enduring melodies and lyrics, is a vibrant if cynical take on the corrupting power of greed and fame.

Due to brief violence, fleeting sexual situations, double entendres, intermittent profanity and an instance of rough language, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
